OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
How many iterations of $n\mapsto \phi(n)+1$ are needed before a prime is reached? Can infinitely many $n$ reach the same prime? What is the density of $n$ which reach any fixed prime?
#409: [ErGr80,p.81]
number theory | 
iterated functions
A problem of Finucane. One can also ask similar questions about $n\mapsto \sigma(n)-1$: do iterates of this always reach a prime? If so, how soon? (It is easily seen that iterates of this cannot reach the same prime infinitely often, since they are non-decreasing.)
This problem is somewhat ambiguously phrased. Let $F(n)$ count the number of iterations of $n\mapsto \phi(n)+1$ before reaching a prime. The number of iterations required is A039651 in the OEIS.
Cambie notes in the comments that $F(n)=o(n)$ is trivial, and $F(n)=1$ infinitely often. Presumably the intended question is to find 'good' upper bounds for $F(n)$.
This is discussed in problem B41 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. 
Additional thanks to: Stijn Cambie and Terence Tao

 I would like to share explicit examples with $F(n)=67$ for Problem #409. Let $F(n)$ be the number of iterations of $n \mapsto \phi(n)+1$ needed to reach a prime, with $F(p)=0$ for prime $p$.
The three checked examples are: 2548851069, 3398468092, 5097702138. All three reach the prime 9005041.
The first trajectory is: 2548851069 -> 1699234045 -> 1359387233 -> 1357766149 -> 1277897537 -> 1091468593 -> 1090197109 -> 1090097101 -> 1054480897 -> 1047381793 -> 1025097029 -> 931906381 -> 794593681 -> 681080293 -> 673559041 -> 651831301 -> 590981521 -> 539896321 -> 539849813 -> 516378061 -> 514939325 -> 410757361 -> 351891889 -> 341863201 -> 333912853 -> 330957761 -> 328495409 -> 298632181 -> 296567041 -> 295161301 -> 291425005 -> 228740929 -> 228693041 -> 221937409 -> 215098801 -> 208160101 -> 207935105 -> 142584049 -> 134196737 -> 129867781 -> 129666413 -> 127631089 -> 126198001 -> 125833973 -> 123955789 -> 116507137 -> 109099585 -> 74426689 -> 71022337 -> 70462981 -> 70202701 -> 64437121 -> 55231813 -> 43699825 -> 30401281 -> 30390193 -> 30089201 -> 28254529 -> 27791281 -> 22566601 -> 22543313 -> 20809201 -> 17808001 -> 17149441 -> 16946161 -> 15534081 -> 10356049 -> 9005041.
The other two merge after one step: 3398468092 -> 1699234045, 5097702138 -> 1699234045
Computation scope:
1. Exhaustive forward sweep: I computed $F(n)$ for every $1 \le n \le 1.5\cdot 10^9$ using a totient sieve and the recurrence $F(n)=F(\phi(n)+1)+1$ for composite $n$. In this exhaustive range the largest value found was $F(n)=66$, at $n=1371524731$.
2. Targeted inverse-totient extension beyond this range: starting from high-$F$ values found by the sweep, I enumerated and verified inverse preimages satisfying $\phi(m)=n-1$ on the frontier. The frontier counts in this run were:
F=63 seeds -> 43 verified F=64 candidates
F=64 candidates -> 10 verified F=65 candidates
F=65 candidates -> 10 verified F=66 candidates
F=66 candidates -> 3 verified F=67 candidates
F=67 candidates -> no inverse preimages found in this run
Thus the search beyond $1.5\cdot 10^9$ was not an exhaustive sweep over all larger integers; it was this targeted inverse-preimage extension from the high-$F$ frontier.

 Two observations bearing on the finiteness conjecture recorded above (that only finitely many integers reach any fixed prime), plus exhaustive data.
1. For 100% of primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, exactly two integers ever reach $p$, namely $p$ and $2p$. Sketch: if $\varphi(n) = p-1 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, write $n = 2^b m$ with $m$ odd; then $v_2(\varphi(n)) = \max(b-1,0) + \sum_{q \mid m} v_2(q-1) = 1$ forces (for $p>3$) either $n \in \{p, 2p\}$ or $n \in \{q^a, 2q^a\}$ with $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ prime, $a \geq 2$, $q^{a-1}(q-1) = p-1$. Since $\varphi(n)+1$ is odd for $n \geq 3$, no even number $\geq 4$ has a preimage, so $2p$ is terminal. Hence unless $p - 1 = q^{a-1}(q-1)$ is solvable, the full basin of $p$ is $\{p, 2p\}$; and the number of exceptional $p \leq x$ is $O(\sqrt{x})$, which is $o(\pi(x))$. This proves the conjectured finiteness (and density zero) for a full-density subfamily of primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Computationally: of the 1632 primes $3 < p < 30000$ with $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, exactly 1620 have basin $\{p, 2p\}$, and the 12 exceptions are precisely $\{7, 19, 43, 163, 487, 1459, 4423, 6163, 14407, 19183, 22651, 26407\}$, matching the characterization.
2. Exhaustive data: for every prime $p < 30000$ the full basin is finite and computed exactly (largest: 5557 elements at $p = 21089$; tallest tree: height 20 at $p = 23509$). Over all $n \leq 10^7$, $\max F(n) = 38$, attained at $n = 7754613$, with decade records $4, 7, 11, 18, 28, 38$ for $n \leq 10^2, \ldots, 10^7$, consistent with $\max_{n \leq x} F(n) \asymp \log x$, and complementing the constructed $F = 67$ examples posted elsewhere in this thread.
3. Two cautions on the conjecture. (a) Dickson's conjecture implies $F$ is unbounded: for each $L$, the forms $q_i = 3^{i-1} 2^{L-i+1} t - 1$ ($1 \leq i \leq L$) and $p = 2^{L+1} t - 3$ form an admissible system, and their simultaneous primality gives $F(3 q_L) = L$ exactly, via $q_{i+1} = (3 q_i + 1)/2$ (verified witnesses through $L = 6$). (b) Empirically, tree growth is a multitype branching process in the type $v_2(m-1)$ (type-1 nodes are sterile by observation 1), and the measured mean-offspring matrix has Perron root $\approx 1.07$ to $1.17$ across scales $10^4$ to $10^7$: marginally supercritical. If the finiteness conjecture holds, it holds near criticality; the alternative reading is that infinite basins exist but are rare.
Full notes with proofs, the exact basin certificates, and verification code: https://github.com/ak56ankit/erdos-409-notes/blob/main/erdos409.pdf . Disclosure per forum rules: this work was done with substantial AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic); I have independently verified the proofs by hand and reproduced all computations myself.

 The page number is 81. Looking at it, the questions for $n \mapsto \sigma(n)-1$ are slightly different from that of $n \mapsto \varphi(n)+1$. The questions are now instead: "Is it true that iterates of this always reach a prime? If so, how soon?". (The question of "can infinitely many $n$ reach the same prime?" is easily seen to be no in this case, because the orbits are now non-decreasing rather than non-increasing; this was first observed by Aristotle.)
